title: Loading, Hauling, and Tipping
body: Every backloading problem, every chipped windscreen, every tire shredded in a pocket, and every dump-edge scare traces back to someone skipping a step in this cycle. Get spotting and tipping discipline right and the rest of the shift runs itself; get it wrong and it shows up as lost tons and NCRs by end of day.
keyPoints: Spotting is a two-signal language: single horn = stop, double horn = go. The excavator bucket is the reference point for reversing in, not the tracks — if the signal and the bucket position disagree, trust the bucket.
Load a straight face, never a pocket. Pockets feel faster in the moment but cost production and chew up tires in hard rock — it's a false shortcut every time.
Two-meter rule on single and double benching: stay off the crest edge, no exceptions, even when the face is running clean.

Backloading has six usual suspects — too many trucks for the cycle, poor fragmentation, spillage cleanup, bad spotting, worn GET, or someone side-loading. If it shows up, don't guess — check the six and fix the actual cause.
No tipping until the berm is built to half the rear wheel height. If it's short, rebuild it before the first truck backs in — that berm is the only thing standing between a truck and a run-off.
apply: Watch the switchback and loading-face positioning calls — trucks coming in flat and excavators following the edge instead of cutting into the heave protects tonnage; a crew that starts repositioning constantly is burning production time for no tons gained.
